title: Elected officials' Online Sharing of Misinformation: Institutional and Ideological Checks
screen_reason: Census of 464,019 Facebook posts by 4,787 U.S. state legislators (2020-2021) with URL domains matched against a 610-source MBFC-derived 'low-factual' list. Reports the share of posts with URLs that were low-factual (0.65%) and the share of legislators who shared any low-factual source (5.6%) - both observed-behaviour SHARING estimates with explicit denominators - plus a within-misinformation hand-validation share (60% of labelled low-factual posts were indeed misleading).

estimates.measure_type: % of U.S. state legislators' Facebook posts containing URLs that linked to a low-factual (misinformation) domain
estimates.value_raw: 1,142 posts with such content (0.65% of all posts with URLs)
estimates.denominator: All Facebook posts containing URLs among the 464,019 posts by 4,787 U.S. state lawmakers collected via CrowdTangle, 2020-2021 (the exact number of posts with URLs is not stated in the text)
estimates.definition: Post whose shared URL resolves to one of the 610 domains on Tai et al. (2025)'s MBFC-derived low-factual reference list
estimates.misinfo_def: "We explore and explain the sharing of misinformation, which we refer to as low-factual content"; operationalised as "Tai et al. (2025)'s low-factual reference that includes 610 sources, originally from Media Bias/Fact Check's (MBFC) ratings. Their reference list focuses on the most misleading information"
estimates.n: All posts with URLs among 464,019 Facebook posts (denominator not stated numerically)
estimates.source_quote: Among the 1,142 posts with such content (0.65% of all posts with URLs), Republicans contributed the vast majority (1,101 posts) compared to Democrats (41 posts) (see Appendix Table A.1).
estimates.ground_truth_detail: 610-domain low-factual reference list from Tai et al. (2025), derived from Media Bias/Fact Check ratings and restricted to the most misleading sources (Fox News, rated 'questionable', is deliberately excluded). MBFC interrater reliability cited from prior work as kappa = 0.82. Coverage check: MBFC-indexed domains account for 51% of the 73,114 shares from 16,854 unique domains, and 61% of the 69,546 shares from domains shared at least 10 times. donaldjtrump.com excluded from downstream analysis as a likely false-positive source.
estimates.moderator_quote: We collected 505,154 raw posts through CrowdTangle from January 1, 2020, to December 31, 2021, in three rounds: April 2022, March 2023, and April 2023. ... After cleaning, we had 464,019 posts from 4,787 state lawmakers, covering 73.1% of those with an official, campaign, or personal Facebook account.
estimates.notes: SHARING (content_share) rather than CONTENT: the denominator is what these actors posted/shared (their own Facebook output with links), and the study frames it as 'sharing of misinformation' by a class of actors. Denominator is posts WITH URLs, not all 464,019 posts - posts without a URL cannot be classified, which the authors flag as an underestimate of the true scope. The abstract's 'less than 1% of legislators' posts overall' is the same finding stated as a bound. year=2021 (end of a 2020-2021 collection window).

estimates.measure_type: % of U.S. state legislators who shared at least one low-factual (misinformation) source on Facebook over 2020-2021
estimates.value_raw: While 94.4% of lawmakers in our analysis did not share any low-factual sources, 5.6% did
estimates.denominator: U.S. state lawmakers in the analysis dataset (4,787 legislators with collected Facebook posts, 73.1% of those with an account; the regression sample is N = 3,262 and the text does not say which of the two the 5.6% is computed on)
estimates.definition: Legislator who shared one or more URLs from the 610-domain low-factual list during 2020-2021
estimates.misinfo_def: "We explore and explain the sharing of misinformation, which we refer to as low-factual content"; operationalised via the MBFC-derived 610-source low-factual domain list
estimates.n: 4,787 state lawmakers (or 3,262 in the regression sample; denominator not disambiguated in text)
estimates.source_quote: While 94.4% of lawmakers in our analysis did not share any low-factual sources, 5.6% did.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same 610-domain MBFC-derived low-factual list; a legislator counts as a sharer if any of their posted URLs matched it. MBFC interrater reliability cited as kappa = 0.82 (Bozarth et al., 2020; Weld et al., 2021).
estimates.moderator_quote: After cleaning, we had 464,019 posts from 4,787 state lawmakers, covering 73.1% of those with an official, campaign, or personal Facebook account.
estimates.notes: Actor-level share (the % of elites who ever shared), the counterpart to the 0.65% item-level share. confidence=medium only because 'lawmakers in our analysis' is not pinned to a number: 4,787 (descriptive dataset) and 3,262 (regression N) are both plausible denominators, and 5.6% of neither is reported as a count.

estimates.measure_type: % of posts already labelled low-factual by the domain list that hand-coding confirmed were genuinely misleading or false (within-misinformation validation)
estimates.value_raw: we sampled 10% (n = 126) of identified low-factual posts ... We found that 60% of labeled low-factual posts were indeed misleading
estimates.denominator: 126 posts, a 10% sample of the 1,142 posts labelled low-factual by the domain list
estimates.definition: Post judged misleading or false by the authors' hand fact-checking against PolitiFact.com, Factcheck.org and similar sites
estimates.misinfo_def: "Their reference list focuses on the most misleading information and has been used to label misinformation from politicians' social media posts."
estimates.source_quote: we sampled 10% (n = 126) of identified low-factual posts and hand-coded their reliability by fact-checking them through websites like PolitiFact.com and Factcheck.org. We found that 60% of labeled low-factual posts were indeed misleading, covering topics such as the 2020 election, abortion, COVID-19 and related vaccines, and climate change policies, and we do not find any cases where legislators held a critical attitude toward the content they share.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Authors hand-coded the reliability of each sampled post by fact-checking it against PolitiFact.com, Factcheck.org and similar sites. Number of coders and inter-coder agreement not reported. The complement (40%) is treated by the authors as the false-positive rate of the domain-level measure in the sensitivity analysis.
estimates.moderator_quote: we sampled 10% (n = 126) of identified low-factual posts and hand-coded their reliability by fact-checking them through websites like PolitiFact.com and Factcheck.org.
estimates.notes: R3 row: falsity computed INSIDE a misinformation-only sample (posts already flagged by the domain list), so within_misinfo_content=true - appendix only, not a prevalence estimate. It is the single most useful validation number in the paper: it implies roughly 40% false positives for domain-level labelling of individual posts, and the authors' own sensitivity analysis is built on that figure.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) JUDGEMENT CALL - state x party extremes not extracted as rows: '33% of Arizona Republicans (9 out of 27) and 16% of Florida Democrats (7 out of 45) shared low-factual content - these are the highest rates observed for Republicans and Democrats, respectively.' These are verbatim part/whole shares with denominators and would pass R8, but they are explicitly selected as the MAXIMA of a state x party cross-tabulation, i.e. double subgroups chosen for being extreme, not the paper's headline prevalence. Extracting them would bias the pooled distribution upward, so I left them out under R4; an adjudicator who reads 'record subgroup rows when they are the paper's headline' more liberally could add two rows. (2) Party split of low-factual posts (Republicans 1,101 vs Democrats 41 of 1,142) is a within-misinformation composition, not a prevalence; the party-specific denominators (posts with URLs by party) are not given, so no rate is derivable without a computation R8 forbids. (3) Per-legislator means are counts, not shares: Arizona n = 360 low-factual posts, mean = 7 per lawmaker; Pennsylvania n = 221, mean = 1; Idaho n = 97, mean = 2; Texas n = 63, mean = 0.4; Table 1 gives Wyoming Republicans 0.32 and Massachusetts Republicans 0, Democrats 0 in both. These are per_capita_intensity values but they are state-level illustrative extremes (the most liberal and most conservative states), so not extracted. (4) Domain-list COVERAGE figures ('MBFC-indexed domains account for 51% of these shares'; '61% are from MBFC-indexed domains' among 69,546 shares from domains shared >= 10 times) measure how much of the link diet the rating list covers, not how much of it is misinformation - MBFC-indexed includes reliable domains - so they are not prevalence estimates. (5) No CONCENTRATION row: 'top sharers within each party' (Appendix Figure A.4) and 'low-factual content is concentrated within a few online communities' are asserted without a paired top-X%/share-of-activity number, so R1 cannot be satisfied. (6) The abstract's 'less than 1% of legislators' posts overall' is a bound on the same quantity as the 0.65% row.

rob.design: CrowdTangle census of U.S. state legislators' Facebook posts, 1 Jan 2020 - 31 Dec 2021, collected in three rounds (Apr 2022, Mar 2023, Apr 2023); 505,154 raw posts cleaned to 464,019 posts from 4,787 lawmakers, 73.1% of those with an official, campaign or personal account (accounts already deleted at collection are missing, a plausible source of downward bias for the most norm-violating legislators). Misinformation measured at URL-domain level against a 610-source MBFC-derived low-factual list; posts without URLs are unclassifiable. Validation reported: MBFC-indexed domains cover 61% of shares from domains shared at least 10 times; hand-coding of a random 10% of flagged posts (n = 126) found 60% genuinely misleading, i.e. ~40% false positives; MBFC interrater reliability quoted from prior literature as kappa = 0.82; sensitivity analysis re-estimating models under assumed false-positive rates of 10-90% with 100 draws each, pooled by Rubin's rules; donaldjtrump.com and outlier individuals/states excluded in robustness checks. No inter-coder reliability reported for the authors' own hand-coding.
rob.item6_quote: We adopted Tai et al. (2025)'s low-factual reference that includes 610 sources, originally from Media Bias/Fact Check's (MBFC) ratings. Their reference list focuses on the most misleading information and has been used to label misinformation from politicians' social media posts.
rob.item10_quote: Among the 1,142 posts with such content (0.65% of all posts with URLs), Republicans contributed the vast majority (1,101 posts) compared to Democrats (41 posts) (see Appendix Table A.1).
